questions.q: The RBI raises interest rates to fight inflation. How does this typically affect the rupee's value against the dollar?
options: The rupee weakens because higher rates scare away foreign investors
The rupee strengthens because higher rates attract foreign investment seeking better returns
The rupee remains unaffected; interest rates only impact bonds, not currency
The rupee weakens because the RBI's action signals economic trouble
questions.explain: Higher interest rates make rupee-denominated assets more attractive to foreign investors, increasing demand for rupees and strengthening its value.

questions.q: An investor puts 50% in Nifty 50, 30% in bonds, and 20% in gold. Market crashes 40%. Why does diversification help here?
options: It prevents any losses because diversified portfolios are immune to crashes
It reduces overall losses by ensuring not all assets fall at the same rate or time
It guarantees the portfolio will only lose 20% (the gold portion)
It increases returns during crashes by automatically rebalancing
questions.explain: Assets move differently in crises—stocks fall hard, but bonds and gold often hold value or rise, so losses are cushioned across the portfolio.

questions.q: A person with poor credit history takes a ₹5 lakh home loan at 9% EMI instead of the standard 7%. Over 20 years, how much extra do they pay?
options: ₹2 lakh extra; credit scores don't meaningfully affect total cost
₹5 lakh extra; the rate difference compounds heavily over time
₹10 lakh+ extra; small rate differences explode in long loans
No extra cost; they just pay slightly more per month
questions.explain: A 2% rate difference on a 20-year loan compounds to over ₹10 lakh in extra interest, showing why credit scores and negotiating rates matter hugely for large loans.

questions.q: A Nifty 50 ETF charges 0.1% annual fee, while an actively managed fund charges 1.2%. If both match Nifty returns before fees over 10 years, which likely gives better returns?
options: The active fund, because the manager picks winning stocks
The ETF, because lower fees compound to significant savings over time
Both give the same returns because they both track Nifty
The active fund, because higher fees mean better quality management
questions.explain: If both deliver same pre-fee returns, the ETF's 1.1% lower annual fee saves roughly ₹50,000+ on ₹5 lakh invested over 10 years—compounding advantage.

questions.q: Raj invests ₹10,000 monthly via SIP in a mutual fund earning 12% yearly. After 20 years, his investment is worth ₹60+ lakh, not ₹24 lakh (contributions). Why?
options: The fund returned more than 12% in some years
Early contributions earn returns for longer; money invested at year 1 grows for 20 years while year 20 money hardly grows
The fund's expense ratio was waived partway through
₹10,000 becomes worth more due to inflation, so contributions are actually worth less
questions.explain: Compounding means earlier SIP installments grow for decades while later ones barely grow, creating exponential wealth; it's not about the fund outperforming.
